lesson_title: The Light That Broke Physics: the Photoelectric Effect
hook_text: A blinding red floodlight can't budge a single electron. One dim blue flicker ejects them instantly. Why?
clip_script: Here is the experiment that broke classical physics. Shine light on a metal and electrons can jump out — but the rules are bizarre. A blinding, powerful red light? Nothing. Not one electron, ever. A dim little blue flicker? Electrons leap out instantly. Brightness loses; colour wins. Einstein saw why, and it won him the Nobel Prize: light is not a smooth wave of energy — it arrives as packets. Photons. Each packet's energy depends only on the light's frequency: blue packets are rich, red packets are poor. And the metal is a club with a bouncer: every electron must pay a fixed exit fee — the work function — and the bouncer takes single payments only. One photon, one electron, no pooling. A million poor red photons are a million separate failures. One rich blue photon pays the fee in full, and the electron walks out keeping the change as speed. That is the whole equation: photon energy equals exit fee plus kinetic energy. And the same packet idea explains why every element glows in its own barcode of sharp colours — electrons dropping between fixed rungs, one photon per drop. That barcode is how we know what stars are made of. One broken rule, one Nobel Prize, one equation — and it is in your Paper 1.
visual_style: A metal surface drawn as a club door with a bouncer; fat red coins bouncing off, one slim blue note opening the door and an electron sprinting out; cut to element barcodes glowing against a starfield.
mood: Mischievous physics heist — the experiment that outsmarted the wave.
pacing: Puzzle posed fast, bouncer reveal in the middle, equation landed clean, cosmic barcode close.
